Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company's participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. China's access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company's first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. Nvidia's deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff. The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States' lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that "to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country." Huang's ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia's data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company's top-line revenue. In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia's dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that's clearly going to change. Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country's domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China's leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China. That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren't serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch. If they can't provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia's market share. Semiconductor and neocloud provider stocks rose on Tuesday in after-hours trading as AI chip-heavy Nvidia (NVDA) reported Q3 results that beat Wall Street's expectations. Peers AMD (AMD) and Broadcom (AVGO) shares rose more than 1% in post-market trading. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM), which manufactures Nvidia's chips, also saw its stock rise 2%. title: Nvidia Delivers the Numbers, but the SEC Adds a New Question - RealMoney Pro
content: Earnings and the guidance were solid, but an SEC investigation reported just before the close means uncertainty isn’t going away. It was another poor day for the market as investors nervously awaited Nvidia’s (NVDA) earnings report. Breadth was weak again, with only around 24% of stocks in the green and more than 720 names hitting new 12-month lows. There is no place to hide in this market right now. Even the defensive names that held up on Monday were sold Tuesday. Investors are raising cash rather than rotating into other sectors. Small-caps were the laggards, with the iShares Russell 2000 ETF (IWM) down about 1.4%. Much of that is due to a lack of interest in the thinnest stocks, which tend to have little support when bids dry up. Stanley Druckenmiller, whom I consider to be one of the greatest investors of all time, said Tuesday that he can’t remember a period when he had less clarity about where we are going to be in 12 months. If he can’t see what is coming, it is no surprise that so many investors are choosing cash over everything else. The good news is that there are many stocks that are still fundamentally solid, but they are being tossed aside with everything else. The lack of selectivity in the selling is what eventually creates the best opportunities. Right before the close, The Wall Street Journal reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia. The focus isn’t clear yet, but it includes whether the company’s disclosures misled investors. I wrote earlier Tuesday that we already knew the bad news and that the uncertainty was about its impact. This is one more piece of bad news, and I didn’t expect it. It grows out of the questions that were already being asked about how Nvidia finances its customers and what it told investors, but an investigation is open-ended, and it will hang over the stock for a while. Nvidia reported earnings of $2.68 a share against expectations of $2.47. Revenue of $115.8 billion was well above the consensus of about $109 billion and topped even the highest estimate on Wall Street. A beat isn’t a big surprise since the quarter closed before the CEO drama began. This report was all about guidance and whether there would be any. Nvidia did provide it, and it expects revenue of about $130 billion in the current quarter, which is above the consensus of around $125 billion. The forecast doesn’t assume any data-center chip sales to China. There is a negative. Nvidia expects its gross margin to fall to between 71% and 72% from close to 75% in the quarter it just reported. Sales are growing, but the company is keeping less of each dollar. The numbers are still solid, and the initial response in the stock is positive, but investors are not chasing the report. The potential for a reversal is high. The report answers the question about how the business is doing right now. It doesn’t answer the questions about the SEC, the search for a new CEO or how the company finances its customers. That is the mix of positives and negatives I was expecting, and it is why I’d rather trade the reaction than make a long-term bet. I’m holding my small position, and I will wait for the reaction in the morning before making any moves. If the stock runs, there are plenty of trapped longs who will be looking for an exit. If it fades, I’ll be measuring the selling against the news to see if there is an opportunity. The larger question is whether this report helps the market find some solid support. That won’t happen immediately, and we have the pricing of the Anthropic IPO Wednesday to deal with next. At the time of publication, Rev Shark was long NVDA.

title: $5.4 Billion In Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) Chips Sit Idle In Hong Kong As Beijing Weighs Dependence On U.S. Silicon - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 17, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis, Politics Roughly 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips are warehoused in Hong Kong, cleared by Washington but still awaiting a green light from Beijing that has yet to come. The White House approved the shipments, yet China’s deliberate silence on import authorization is telling analysts something significant about how Beijing calculates its long-term technology strategy. Karson Elmgren, research manager at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy in Washington, draws a pointed conclusion: “To me, this suggests that China does not view short-term advantages as decisive and is confident in its ability to replace US chips over the medium term.” At $27,000 per unit and with estimated Chinese demand running to 2 million chips, the H200 alone represents a potential $5.4 billion revenue stream for Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), making Beijing’s hesitation all the more striking to outside observers. The H200 falls short of Nvidia’s highest-performance tier, yet it outpaces competing Chinese products by a meaningful margin, which has made it commercially attractive despite the fraught geopolitical environment surrounding it. That environment grew considerably more fraught after Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO, triggered by revelations of extramarital relationships, one of which involved a businesswoman whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying on behalf of Beijing. Huang, 63 and Taiwan-born, had cultivated near-celebrity standing in China and served as a key AI adviser to President Donald Trump during his second term, consistently advocating for fewer restrictions on chip sales to Chinese buyers. Beijing flatly denied orchestrating any effort to compromise Huang, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning stating on November 13: “China has consistently opposed the misuse of export control measures that jeopardize the stability of global industrial and supply chains, as this is not in the interest of either party.” State media outlet Global Times was blunter still, running an editorial that asked: “Jensen Huang cheated on his wife. What does that have to do with China?” — accusing U.S. journalists of constructing a “Hollywood thriller” without “hard evidence to back up the central allegations.” On Weibo, Chinese users were equally skeptical, with one attributing Huang’s exit to “the result of political maneuvering within the United States” and another dismissing the entire narrative by asking: “Could a love affair really cause Mr. Huang to resign? Isn’t this plot a little too melodramatic?” The scandal has nonetheless accelerated Washington’s push for tighter controls, with the administration said to be crafting additional restrictions designed to close loopholes that currently allow Chinese firms to obtain advanced American semiconductors. Those controls operate against a backdrop of systematic Chinese investment in domestic chip alternatives, with military hardware leading the way — the Chengdu J-20 fighter jet and the Dongfeng-41 intercontinental ballistic missile both run exclusively on Chinese-made chips. Tiantian Wang of the Harbin Institute of Technology argues this approach serves a dual purpose, writing that domestic chips “effectively mitigates the risks of cyberattacks by foreign actors” while also fulfilling a national security imperative she described as “strengthening autonomy and control over national defense and critical infrastructure.” Wang contends that China has engineered “a closed ecosystem that encompasses data, algorithms, computing power, and chips, thereby reducing systemic dependence on foreign chips such as Nvidia.” A critical gap remains, however: China still lacks the lithography equipment required to manufacture leading-edge chips at commercial scale, after ASML, the Dutch machinery giant, halted advanced machine exports to Beijing under sustained U.S. pressure. The Center for Technology and Statecraft warned that had China continued importing ASML systems at the pace it maintained through 2024 and 2025, “its annual production could be sufficient to wipe out much of the US lead and, under certain scenarios, even surpass it.” Consulting firm Deloitte notes that Beijing is responding with a sweeping capital commitment, with the strategy’s “focus on supporting companies through long-term capital provision and research-oriented incentives to build sustainable innovation in key technologies.” Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, who chairs the Communist Party’s Commission on Science and Technology, carries primary responsibility for translating that investment into the kind of technological leap that could, over time, render the chip import debate moot entirely. The central question facing Ding is whether China can sustain dependence on American silicon long enough to develop domestic alternatives capable of matching them — a calculation that those 600,000 waiting chips in Hong Kong now embody in concrete form. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA, XETRA:NVD) delivered another strong quarterly performance, with revenue more than doubling year over year and its outlook for the current quarter topping Wall Street expectations as demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure continued to drive growth. The chipmaker reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and ahead of analyst estimates of $109.3 billion. Adjusted earnings per share rose 111% to $2.68, beating the consensus forecast of $2.47, while adjusted gross margin improved 140 basis points year over year to 74.9%. Data Center remained the company's largest growth engine, generating $107.6 billion in revenue, up 110% from the prior year and ahead of expectations of $101.9 billion. Hyperscale revenue reached $60.1 billion, up 71% year over year and above the $54.1 billion forecast. Revenue from AI cloud providers, industrial customers and enterprises totalled $47.5 billion, a 195% increase, although it fell slightly short of the $48.4 billion estimate. The company also reported $2.4 billion in shipments of Hopper data center chips to China during the quarter. Looking ahead, Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $130 billion, plus or minus 3%, compared with analyst expectations of $124.4 billion. It expects adjusted gross margin of between 71% and 72%, against the market forecast of 71.7%, while adjusted operating expenses are projected to reach approximately $10.7 billion. A key development was the launch of its Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, which the company said generated nearly $20 billion in revenue during its launch quarter, marking the fastest product ramp in its history. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater," said Colette Kress, interim CEO and executive vice president and chief financial officer. Nvidia also highlighted growing commitments across its supply chain and infrastructure operations. Supply commitments climbed to $390 billion from $279 billion in the previous quarter, largely reflecting multi-year memory purchases. Cloud service agreements and data center lease commitments increased to $102 billion from $74 billion. The company also disclosed $20 billion in equity investment commitments, primarily focused on frontier AI laboratories and infrastructure financiers. Nvidia shares rose about 2.7% in after-hours trading following the results. Concern over the future of the tech sector dragged down stock markets Tuesday, as traders sold off shares linked to the AI industry ahead of an earnings report from crisis-hit chip giant Nvidia. The company was set to announce more bumper revenues and profits in its report, due out after Wall Street closed, but its longer-term growth is shrouded in uncertainty after the United States moved to tighten restrictions on Chinese access to chips. Jensen Huang resigned as head of Nvidia last week over revelations of an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, and wider suspicions her firm was funneling Nvidia products into China. The Nasdaq, the benchmark US tech index, fell a further 0.74 percent Tuesday. "Beyond the usual focus on results, forward guidance, and data center demand, investors will be closely watching the company's first earnings call with Colette Kress as interim CEO following Jensen Huang's abrupt departure," Adam Turnquist at LPL Financial said. "With Huang widely viewed as 'irreplaceable,' attention will center on the leadership transition and the board's timeline for naming a permanent CEO," he added. "Shares have been pressured by the double-edged sword of growing concerns over an AI slowdown and uncertainty surrounding Huang's departure." Huang said Tuesday he was hoping for a comeback, fuelled by support from US President Donald Trump, but that outcome is highly uncertain. Adding to the downbeat mood was news that the US Commerce Department had moved to shut a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely. The markets were also trying to fathom the consequences of AI firm Anthropic's initial public offering, which is expected in New York on Thursday. The share sale is expected to value the firm, which makes the Claude chatbot, as high as $1.4 trillion, which would make it one of the world's most valuable companies. While Anthropic is widely seen as the leader for AI products, Nvidia has been dubbed the "central bank" of the industry for its investments in startups and providing backstops on loans. By the end of the week, traders are hoping to have more certainty about the commercial future of a technology that has been long on hype but short on profitable products. Traders, meanwhile, sold off some technology-adjacent stock -- Nvidia's price plunged in morning deals before partly recovering. On Wall Street, all three major indexes backed up Monday's steep losses with more negative numbers. The Dow Jones shed 1.64 percent. Trading in Europe was sluggish all day and tapered dramatically by close, with all three major indexes finishing down. Frankfurt led the way with 2.1 percent losses, and the pattern was similar across Asia. title: Prediction: These Will Be Nvidia’s and AMD’s Stock Prices by the End of 2027 (Hint: Only 1 Is a Buy). - The Motley Fool
content: AMD's stock has a ton of growth priced into it already. Nvidia (NVDA -0.44%) has had a rough few weeks with CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang resigning. That has cratered the stock, which is now down significantly from its all-time high. Nvidia's loss has been AMD's (AMD -0.17%) gain. The rival chipmaker’s stock has risen 16% since November began, while Nvidia's is down nearly 20%. AMD investors couldn't have been more pleased. There's also the potential that some Nvidia investors are shifting funds into AMD shares to maintain their AI exposure without the mess of a CEO transition, which is a valid premise. However, I think most of the Nvidia saga will be wrapped up by the time 2027 ends, and the stock market will have returned to valuing both businesses for what they are, rather than based on how headlines are influencing them. So, what do I expect each stock to be trading at by the end of 2027? I think you'll be very surprised. Leadership matters in a company. That's why the news of Huang’s rapid exit was so jarring to many investors. He has been the only CEO in its history, and he was instrumental in building the company into what it is today. Without him at the helm, some investors aren't as confident in Nvidia's prospects. Still, Huang didn't do everything at Nvidia. Countless others helped build Nvidia into what it is, many of its longtime leaders are still there, and one could take over next. Nvidia's products remain superior to AMD's, and the company still has a wide moat thanks to the ubiquity of its CUDA software platform, which allows its GPUs to be programmed for whatever uses its customers have in mind. Because so much early AI work was done on CUDA, and because so many developers are comfortable in it, shifting out of the Nvidia ecosystem can be a chore. While AMD's GPUs are growing more popular, they're only being deployed in certain applications. Meanwhile, Nvidia still holds a commanding market-share lead in data center GPUs and is still delivering faster sales growth. Nvidia has recently delivered particularly impressive growth given how large its revenue base is relative to AMD's, but the market isn't giving the chipmaker credit for it. With 2026 nearly wrapped up, it's OK for investors to start looking ahead to 2027. Next year, Wall Street analysts expect Nvidia's revenue to grow at a 67% pace. While some may discount that growth rate given what's going on in the C-suite, I don't think that's a wise investment move. The reality is that Nvidia's largest clients already know what they're going to spend on chips next year, and they've let Nvidia know so these products are ready to go when they need them. During the Q2 earnings call, management gave guidance for 70% revenue growth in 2027. It's rare to see a company issue guidance for the upcoming year so far in advance. The only reason why Nvidia would do that is if it had high visibility into revenue, and nothing that has happened over the past few weeks will likely change its outlook for 2027. According to the analyst community, AMD's growth rate is expected to exceed Nvidia's. Analysts project AMD will grow its revenue at an 84% clip. That would be a strong outperformance if AMD can pull it off, but considering its much smaller sales base, it's not growing nearly fast enough to make a big dent in Nvidia's lead. Regardless of what transpires next year, the reality is that AMD's expected growth has already been priced into its stock, while Nvidia's hasn't. AMD is over three times more expensive than Nvidia based on next year's earnings projections. That's a huge price mismatch, and I think it's a bit absurd that AMD trades at that much of a premium when their growth rates are fairly similar. While I agree that AMD deserves a premium right now because its CEO is still in place, Nvidia has technological advantages and a massive market-share lead that cannot be discounted. Given how expensive AMD stock is, I forecast that its stock will be flat over the next year and will still trade at around just under $600 per share at the end of 2027. Meanwhile, I wouldn't be surprised to see Nvidia's price-to-earnings ratio double to 20, which would also imply a stock price double that of today's level, about $330 per share. US chip giant Nvidia on Tuesday ruled out any comeback for ousted CEO Jensen Huang, who was forced out in a spy scandal, and reported that it had doubled revenue in the third quarter to more than $115 billion, beating expectations. Huang sought to be reinstated despite resigning last week over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, but his successor -- interim CEO Colette Kress -- said that it was now "business as usual" at the company as it charts a way ahead without him. Harvey Jones, the chair of the company's board, said in an earnings call that "the Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Investors scoured the upbeat results for evidence that the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the Nvidia crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies. "Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," Kress said in her first remarks since being appointed by the board last week. She forecast stronger revenue growth of 75 percent in next fiscal year, up from 70 percent. Huang's bid on Tuesday to get his job back was the latest twist for the company at the center of an AI boom that has propelled markets to record highs and boosted global economic growth. The recent upheaval has battered shares of Nvidia -- which has lost $700 billion in market value since the scandal broke -- and Huang is to be questioned by US lawmakers on December 1 over national security concerns. A charismatic promoter of AI, his fall triggered immediate calls from Elon Musk and others for his return, and even President Donald Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Huang back at Nvidia, downplaying the espionage allegations. "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said, hours before the earnings release. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." As the spy scandal deepened, Washington on Monday announced new restrictions on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing. The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which starts this week in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Under Washington's new rules, data centers anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes. The rules also require licenses to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil -- countries the US Commerce Department says present a "higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips. The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China. While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang's affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice. His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed -- a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls. Investors are watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang's aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies. Huang on Tuesday sounded a note of contrition in his statement, saying "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life." title: NVIDIA Board of Directors Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee - NVIDIA Newsroom
content: NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that the Board of Directors has established the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, a new standing committee responsible for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. NVIDIA’s existing National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team will report directly to the Committee and to Interim CEO, Colette Kress, on day-to-day operations. The Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and will also include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. It will meet at least quarterly, including with management and in executive session. The Committee will oversee the Company’s ongoing efforts to enhance its internal National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team, and work closely with independent third-party experts in law, national security and global trade compliance. “NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security. As the world’s leading advanced computing company, NVIDIA has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation,” said Harvey Jones, Chairman of NVIDIA’s Board of Directors. The decision to create this new committee reflects the Board’s further commitment to enhance its engagement with relevant government stakeholders, and to demonstrate the highest standards of governance and oversight.

title: Trump’s accounts traded up to $97.5 million in Nvidia as Huang gained White House access - CNBC
content:
President Donald Trump has had plenty of reason to cheer the rise of Nvidia. The chipmaker helped propel the stock market that Trump is fond of touting. Its billionaire co-founder, Jensen Huang, became one of the president’s favorite businessmen. And by the end of last year, Nvidia had become one of Trump’s three largest individual stock holdings, worth between $12.5 million and $58 million, up from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier. Since returning to the White House, Trump’s investment accounts have bought or sold Nvidia shares at least 103 times — transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, according to a new CNBC analysis of his annual and periodic financial disclosures, which were most recently updated through August. By midday Monday, Trump’s Nvidia stake, based on the value he reported holding in August, would be worth $4.5 million to $57.7 million with stock priced around $157. But the filings give broad dollar ranges for holdings rather than the number of shares, leaving his current stake unclear. Now, Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday, following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees, has put those trades back in the spotlight. Among them was a sale of $500,001 to $1 million on May 18, the first Monday after Trump returned from a state visit to China with Huang. Five days earlier, before Huang boarded Air Force One during a refueling stop in Alaska, Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence concerning Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, The New York Times reported. Trump on Monday denied being briefed. Asked about the reported briefing from Rubio, Trump said, “I haven’t heard that,” adding that he did not know whether the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy. The president’s financial accounts also bought smaller amounts of Nvidia shares in the days immediately before and after the May 18 sale, part of a broader trading blitz. Such flurries have defined his second term: Trump disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone, compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term, according to CNBC’s analysis. A White House spokesperson told CNBC independent advisors manage Trump’s portfolio without his input. Trump Organization spokesperson Kimberly Benza said the arrangement is designed to “avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest.” The disclosures offer no evidence Trump directed the trades or that his advisors had access to classified intelligence. Trump has long used the stock market as a scorecard for the economy, touting its record highs — sometimes when highs have not actually been reached — despite the turbulence caused by his tariffs and the Iran war. “Look, we have the highest stock market we’ve ever had,” Trump told ESPN commentator and political talk show host Stephen A. Smith on Thursday when pressed about Republicans’ midterm losses. Nvidia alone accounted for about 13.5% of the S&P 500′s 2026 gains through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth that looked at how chip stocks have driven the year’s performance. Huang’s rise in Trump’s Washington has been nearly as striking as Nvidia’s on Wall Street. The two have met or appeared together at least 15 times since Trump returned to office, according to a CNBC review of public records and news reports. Huang in June told The Associated Press that Trump even “calls me in the middle of the night.” At Trump’s Jan. 20, 2025, inauguration, several Silicon Valley titans occupied prime seats, but Huang wasn’t there. The two men had never met. That changed on Jan. 31, 2025, when Huang visited the White House, capping a bruising week for Nvidia: Chinese AI startup DeepSeek had wiped $593 billion off the company’s market value in a single day, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. Two days before the meeting, Trump’s money managers bought between $1 million and $5 million in Nvidia stock. For Huang, much of the relationship hinged on access to China. In April 2025, the administration effectively halted sales of Nvidia’s H20 chips to China, prompting a $4.5 billion charge, according to an SEC filing. Huang argued that withholding U.S. chips would only accelerate China’s development of its own. The administration eventually relented. After another meeting with Trump in July 2025, Huang announced from Beijing that Nvidia expected to resume H20 sales. A week after Trump confirmed an August 2025 deal calling for 15% of the revenue from the company’s chip sales to China to go to the U.S. government, his accounts also bought between $5 million and $25 million in Nvidia stock, one of several large tech investments that day. Huang was also becoming a fixture of Trump’s international diplomacy, joining him in Saudi Arabia and the U.K. Nvidia, already a $1 million donor to Trump’s inaugural fund, would pledge another $25 million to his planned White House ballroom on condition of anonymity, The Washington Post first reported. But behind the scenes, intelligence officials first briefed Trump last fall on Huang’s relationship with the woman suspected of spying for China, The New York Times reported. Trump nevertheless continued to ease restrictions on Nvidia’s business in China, announcing Dec. 8 that the company could sell its more powerful H200 chips. His accounts had sold as much as $1 million in Nvidia stock four days earlier and bought more the day after. In the first eight months of 2026, Trump’s accounts made another 38 Nvidia trades worth a combined $9.4 million to $28.3 million, according to CNBC’s analysis. A disclosure released Oct. 8 — the day Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science — showed purchases of up to $1.6 million and sales of up to $1 million in August alone. Trump stood by Huang as Nvidia’s board weighed his future last week, urging him to fight to keep his job, the Times reported. With Huang out and Nvidia’s shares tumbling, Trump described him Thursday as a “tremendous talent” who was “going through hell” — in the same interview in which he boasted of the market’s record highs. Trump is already floating a comeback for Huang, telling reporters Monday that reinstating him “certainly isn’t a bad idea.” But Nvidia’s board is not considering his return, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. Nvidia (NVDA) stock fell 4% on Monday as investors weighed tighter US restrictions on overseas access to advanced AI semiconductors and a report that supporters of Jensen Huang are lobbying for his return to the chip heavyweight following his abrupt resignation last week. Huang has discussed returning as CEO with confidants, the Financial Times reported Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. "Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen," the person said, adding that Huang supported the effort. On Monday, CNBC reported that the board was not considering bringing Huang back to the company. Meanwhile, SpaceX (SPCX) and Tesla (TSLA) CEO Elon Musk has come out in support of Huang, writing on X last Friday, "A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen, and I'm signing it too." On Saturday, Musk said, "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract. Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." The push to bring Huang back comes days after the FT reported that Nvidia's board had approached Arm Holdings (ARM) CEO Rene Haas as it searches for a successor. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO during the search. Yorkville's Dan Ives said that while no "one individual can replace Jensen as CEO," any talk of "Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/Board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles." This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. Days earlier, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife but did not disclose how many affairs he had or identify those involved. Recent reports have raised concerns about whether restricted semiconductors were being diverted to China and if sensitive US information had been sent to Beijing. The developments have also sent shockwaves through the AI industry, where Nvidia has played a central role in building the ecosystem. The company has become a bellwether for the AI trade and has invested in key parts of the industry, including large language model development, energy, optics, and cloud providers. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results Tuesday after the bell in what will be the company's first earnings call without Huang. Nvidia stock declined more than 12% last week, closing below a $4 trillion market cap. At least 10 Wall Street analysts have recently downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold, with many citing, in part, increased scrutiny in Washington and succession uncertainty.
